extracted.intended_audience: readers of Montaigne / educated general readers interested in moral philosophy and personal essays
extracted.subtask_description: A Renaissance-era personal/philosophical essay (Montaigne) exploring human behaviour, virtues, customs, and moral examples through anecdotes and reflection. The page is an edition of Montaigne's Essays covering topics such as constancy, fate, courage, monstrous births, and anger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make life correspond with doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: He who erected so pleasant a knowledge upon ignorance, endeavoured ... to make his life correspond with his doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: philosophers who maintain their doctrines in behaviour — e.g., a man who, if he began a discourse, would always end what he had to say though the person had gone away; one who walked and never stopped for impediments; who suffered incisions and cauteries without wincing. The text uses these anecdotes to show the ideal of living consistently with professed beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain indifference and persevering constancy
rubrics_metrics.description: He maintained the imbecility of human judgment to be so extreme as to be incapable of any choice or inclination, and would have it perpetually wavering and suspended, considering and receiving all things as indifferent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical manifestations: preserving from fear, not avoiding impediments, resisting pain without visible emotion. The essay notes that bringing the soul to such imaginations is one thing; joining effects and making them habitual is almost incredible, and gives examples and counterexamples to illustrate the difficulty of perfect indifference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjoin imagination with effects; make virtue habitual
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Tis something to bring the soul to these imaginations; ‘tis more to join the effects, and yet not impossible; but to conjoin them with such perseverance and constancy as to make them habitual, is certainly, in attempts so remote from the common usage, almost incredible to be done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes theoretical acceptance from sustained practical behavior; examples of persons (gymnosophists, Cybele priests) who institutionalize premeditated death show how habit and social framework can make extreme practices possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premeditated self-sacrifice as cultural/practical custom
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of customs where wives or priests prepare and perform self-destruction as a social or religious practice (e.g., Indian wives burying themselves with husbands; gymnosophists and Cybele priests preparing funeral piles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance is largely descriptive: when an action is embedded in ritual and social expectation, it becomes conceivable and practiced; the essay distinguishes culturally sanctioned premeditation from sudden, irrational acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreknowledge does not necessitate events (knowledge ≠ causation)
rubrics_metrics.description: That which we see come to pass, as we do, and as God Himself also does ... is not to compel an event: that is, we see because things do fall out, but things do not fall out because we see: events cause knowledge, but knowledge does not cause events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument applied to debates about fate: God’s prescience catalogs causes including accidental and voluntary ones; free will remains. The essay then examines how belief in fate influences behavior (e.g., soldiers encouraged by fatalism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief in fatalism can encourage extreme courage or recklessness
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong and lively faith in a prefixed term of days draws along with it actions of the same kind (e.g., Bedouins going naked to war, some Turks attributing immunity to fate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne notes that whether genuinely believed or used as an excuse, fatalistic belief can be employed to justify or foster daring conduct; but he questions how easily people are persuaded and shows mixed examples of effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions must match words for credibility and authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Saying is a different thing from doing; we are to consider the sermon apart and the preacher apart. A man whose morals are good may have false opinions, and a wicked man may preach truth ... saying, when the actions follow, is of greater authority and efficacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: philosophers whose deeds reinforce their teachings (Plutarch, Cleomenes, Eudamidas). The essay stresses that writers/speakers should be judged in part by their conduct, and that concordance of word and deed strengthens persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: True signs of anger are physical manifestations, not mere words
rubrics_metrics.description: Plutarch calmly answered: 'How, ruffian, by what dost thou judge that I am now angry? Does either my face, my colour, or my voice give any manifestation of my being moved? ... Do I start? Do I tremble with fury? For those, I tell thee, are the true signs of anger.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes true anger (observable by face, colour, voice, trembling) from mere complaint. Use of measured demeanor to show lack of anger and to keep judgment clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defer action while under passion; avoid acting in anger
rubrics_metrics.description: When the pulse beats, and we feel emotion in ourselves, let us defer the business; things will indeed appear otherwise to us when we are calm and cool. ‘Tis passion that then commands, ‘tis passion that speaks, and not we.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to punishments, chastisements, and important business: do not whip or make final decisions while angry; faults looked at in passion appear larger; delay leads to a calmer, fairer response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chastisement should be weighed, discreet, purposeful, and reach the offender
rubrics_metrics.description: Chastisements that are inflicted with weight and discretion are much better received and with greater benefit by him who suffers ... they be not angry to no purpose, but make sure that their reprehension reach him with whom they are offended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice to those in authority: avoid lavishing anger on every occasion (it lessens effect); ensure scolding is directed at the true offender; avoid scolding when person is absent or long after the fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid habitual/public angry outbursts (they lose effect and harm discipline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rash and incessant scolding runs into custom, and renders itself despised; they attack his shadow, and drive the storm in a place where no one is either chastised or concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Angry displays rehearsed publicly or habitually become theatrical and ineffective; use anger sparingly and targetedly for corrective impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open vices are less dangerous than concealed ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Omnia vitia in aperto leviora sunt: et tunc perniciosissima, quum simulata sanitate subsident. — 'All vices are less dangerous when open to be seen, and then most pernicious when they lurk under a dissembled good nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne counsels candidness: he would rather reveal passions or faults than brood over them secretly, because concealed vices are more harmful to the self and community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feigning anger may be a pragmatic household tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes also it falls out that I put on a seeming anger, for the better governing of my house, without any real emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges a pragmatic distinction between genuine passion and performed anger used instrumentally to govern servants; but cautions about internal cost of constant masking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anger can be an instrument of virtue or valour in military contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle says, that anger sometimes serves for arms to virtue and valour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne allows that anger is more excusable in soldiers where it can fuel necessary boldness; context matters in assessing the morality or utility of anger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passion-driven judgments produce injustice; beware rash decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Example of Piso: moved by fury he condemned a soldier to death who seemed guilty; when the soldier’s companion returned, Piso’s shame and spite redoubled, leading him to create additional victims — a caution on angry rashness producing further harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a warning that decisions made in haste or passion can compound injustice; emphasizes need for reflection and restraint in adjudication and punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and nurture of children shape the state; parental power should be constrained
rubrics_metrics.description: The most of our civil governments ... leave ... to every one the ordering of their wives and children, according to their own foolish and indiscreet fancy; and the Lacedaemonian and Cretan are almost the only governments that have committed the education of children to the laws. Who does not see that in a state all depends upon their nurture and bringing up?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne uses this as a criterion for political/social organization: child-rearing affects the future citizenry, so systems that leave upbringing solely to parents risk producing ill-conditioned members of the commonwealth; he favors institutional oversight of education.
